title: Type Aliases
summary: A **type alias** uses the `type` keyword to give a name to any type — a primitive, a union, an object shape, or a function signature — so you can reuse it instead of repeating the definition.

subtopics.title: The type keyword
subtopics.explanation: type Name = SomeType creates a new name for an existing type. It introduces no new type — it's just an alias the compiler substitutes wherever you use it. Aliases are erased at compile time and add nothing to the runtime bundle.
subtopics.example:
type ID = number;
const userId: ID = 42;

subtopics.title: Aliasing primitives
subtopics.explanation: You can alias a primitive to give it meaning: type UserId = string makes a plain string self-documenting. Note these are structurally the same — a UserId and any string are interchangeable — but the name communicates intent to readers.
subtopics.example:
type Email = string;
function send(to: Email) {}

subtopics.title: Aliasing unions
subtopics.explanation: Aliases are especially valuable for unions, which interfaces cannot express. type Status = 'active' | 'archived' | 'pending' names a closed set of allowed values once, so you can reuse it everywhere instead of repeating the union.

subtopics.title: Aliasing object shapes
subtopics.explanation: An alias can name an object type: type User = { id: number; name: string }. This works much like an interface for plain object shapes and is a common way to type props, records, and config objects.
subtopics.example: type User = { id: number; name: string };

subtopics.title: Aliasing function types
subtopics.explanation: You can alias a function signature so callbacks and handlers share one definition: type Handler = (event: string) => void. Reusing the alias keeps callback types consistent across an API.

subtopics.title: Generic type aliases
subtopics.explanation: Aliases can take type parameters, just like generic functions: type Box<T> = { value: T } or type Nullable<T> = T | null. This lets one alias adapt to many element types while staying type-safe.
subtopics.example:
type Nullable<T> = T | null;
const x: Nullable<string> = null;

subtopics.title: Alias vs interface (brief)
subtopics.explanation: Both can name an object shape. Interfaces are best for object/class contracts and support declaration merging and extends; type aliases additionally cover unions, tuples, primitives, and function types. A common guideline: interface for objects you may extend, type for everything else. (See the dedicated interface vs type topic.)
subtopics.example:
interface User { id: number; }
type Status = 'on' | 'off';

foundations.overview: A type alias gives a reusable name to any type using the type keyword. Instead of repeating { id: number; name: string } or 'active' | 'archived' across a codebase, you define it once and reference the name. Aliases work for primitives, unions, objects, functions, tuples, and generics.
foundations.formalDefinition: A type alias is a named reference to a type, declared with type Name = Type. It does not create a new distinct type — it's a substitutable name for the underlying type — and it is erased at compile time.
foundations.whyItMatters: Aliases make code DRY and self-documenting, and they're the only way to name unions, tuples, and complex composed types. Understanding when to use a type alias versus an interface is a frequent beginner interview question.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a type alias like a const for types: you give a long or repeated type expression a short, meaningful name, and the compiler expands it wherever the name appears.
foundations.browserPerspective: Type aliases are purely compile-time. They're erased during compilation, so the emitted JavaScript contains no trace of them and they add zero runtime cost.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Naming React prop types (type Props = {...}), API response shapes, status unions (type Status = 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'), reusable callback signatures, and generic helpers like Nullable<T> or ApiResponse<T>.
foundations.businessImpact: Reusable, named types reduce duplication and drift between definitions, lowering the chance of mismatched shapes causing bugs in features that share data.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Defining a shape once and referencing it everywhere means a change is made in one place and type-checked across all usages, easing refactors.
foundations.performanceImpact: None at runtime (erased). Very large unions or deeply nested alias compositions can slow the type-checker/editor, so keep composed aliases reasonable.
commonUseCases: Typing React props and config objects
Generic helpers like Nullable<T> or ApiResponse<T>

commonMisconceptions.myth: A type alias creates a brand-new, distinct type.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's just a name for an existing type; aliased primitives are structurally identical and interchangeable with the underlying type.

commonMisconceptions.myth: type aliases and interfaces are completely interchangeable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only interfaces support declaration merging; only type aliases can name unions, tuples, primitives, and function types directly. They overlap mainly for object shapes.

debuggingLab.title: Repeating a union instead of aliasing it
debuggingLab.symptom: The same status union is written inline in several places; adding a new value means editing every spot, and one was missed.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The union 'active' | 'archived' is duplicated inline. When the domain gains a 'pending' value, each copy must be updated by hand; missing one (here, badge) leaves an inconsistent, error-prone contract that the compiler can't help keep in sync.
commonMistakes: Copy-pasting the same union into multiple signatures.
Editing one copy of a duplicated type and forgetting the others.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Define the union once as a type alias and reference it everywhere.

theory.question: What is a type alias and what can it name?
theory.directAnswer: A type alias, declared with the type keyword, gives a reusable name to any type — a primitive, a union, a tuple, an object shape, or a function signature. It doesn't create a new distinct type; it's a substitutable name the compiler expands wherever it's used, and it's erased at compile time.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A named reference to an existing type, written type Name = Type.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To avoid repeating type definitions and to name composed types (unions, tuples, function types) that interfaces can't express directly.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler substitutes the alias with its underlying type at every usage and erases the alias on emit.

theory.whyImportant: Aliases are foundational for DRY, self-documenting types and are the only way to name unions and tuples — a core beginner topic.
theory.realWorldExample: type Status = 'loading' | 'success' | 'error' names a UI state union reused across components and reducers.

nestedTopics.title: Naming unions
nestedTopics.explanation: Aliases can name a union of literals or types, which interfaces cannot.

nestedTopics.title: Function aliases
nestedTopics.explanation: type Handler = (e: string) => void names a callback signature.

nestedTopics.title: Erased at runtime
nestedTopics.explanation: Aliases add no runtime code; they're compile-time only.

followUps.question: Does aliasing a primitive create a new type?
followUps.answer: No — type UserId = string is structurally identical to string and interchangeable with it; the name only conveys intent.

followUps.question: Can an interface name a union?
followUps.answer: No — only a type alias can name a union; interfaces describe object/class shapes.

theory.question: What is a generic type alias and when would you use one?
theory.directAnswer: A generic type alias takes one or more type parameters, like type Box<T> = { value: T } or type Nullable<T> = T | null. You use it to define a reusable shape that adapts to different element types while staying type-safe — for example a Result<T, E> type or an ApiResponse<T> used across many endpoints.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An alias parameterized by type variables that are filled in at the point of use.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To name a reusable, type-safe pattern once instead of duplicating it per concrete type.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When you reference Box<number>, the compiler substitutes T = number and expands the alias for that usage.

theory.whyImportant: It connects aliases to generics and shows you can build reusable, parameterized types — common in shared utility code.
theory.realWorldExample: type ApiResponse<T> = { data: T; ok: boolean } types every endpoint's response with the right data shape.

nestedTopics.title: Type parameters
nestedTopics.explanation: Box<T> introduces a placeholder T filled at use.

nestedTopics.title: Composition
nestedTopics.explanation: Generic aliases combine with unions, e.g. Nullable<T> = T | null.

followUps.question: How is a generic type alias different from a generic interface?
followUps.answer: Both can be generic over object shapes, but a generic type alias can also parameterize unions, tuples, and function types, which an interface cannot.

scenario.question: A codebase repeats the object shape { id: number; name: string } inline across many functions. A teammate asks whether to use a type alias or an interface to centralize it. What do you advise?
scenario.directAnswer: Either works for a plain object shape — define it once and reference it. I'd lean toward an interface if this shape represents a contract that other types may extend or that a class implements, since interfaces support extends and declaration merging. I'd use a type alias if it's a simple shape or may later become part of a union. The key win is centralizing it so a change happens in one place.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Choosing between a type alias and an interface to name a shared object shape.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To eliminate duplicated inline shapes and keep the definition in one type-checked place.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Both name the shape; interfaces add merging/extends, type aliases add union/tuple/function flexibility.

scenario.whyImportant: This is the canonical type-vs-interface decision interviewers ask about, and centralizing shapes is a common real refactor.

nestedTopics.title: DRY shapes
nestedTopics.explanation: Define once, reference everywhere, edit in one place.

nestedTopics.title: Extensibility
nestedTopics.explanation: Interfaces extend and merge; aliases compose with unions.

followUps.question: When does the choice actually matter?
followUps.answer: When you need declaration merging or class implements (favor interface) or need a union/tuple/function type (must use a type alias).

coding.question: Define a generic type alias Result<T> that represents either a success (with data) or a failure (with an error message), then write a function that returns it.
coding.thoughtProcess: I want a discriminated union so callers can narrow on a tag. I'll define Result<T> as a union of two object shapes sharing an ok field: { ok: true; data: T } and { ok: false; error: string }. This is exactly the kind of thing a type alias can express but an interface cannot. The function returns Result<number>, and checking r.ok narrows to the right branch.
coding.lineByLine: Result<T> is a generic type alias naming a discriminated union with an ok tag. parseAge returns Result<number>: a failure object when parsing fails, a success object otherwise. Checking r.ok narrows the union so r.data (number) or r.error (string) is accessed safely — something a type alias's union expresses cleanly.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) for the parse and branch.

alternativeApproaches.title: Throwing instead of Result
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Throwing loses the typed error path; a Result alias makes both outcomes explicit and type-checked.

followUps.question: Why can't an interface express Result<T> directly?
followUps.answer: Result<T> is a union of two shapes; interfaces describe a single object shape and can't name a union, so a type alias is required.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Type aliases form a project's shared vocabulary: status unions, API response wrappers (ApiResponse<T>), Result<T, E> types, and named callback signatures. Centralizing these in a types module gives the whole codebase a consistent, single-source-of-truth set of shapes.
productionDeepDive.performance: Zero runtime cost — aliases are erased. At scale, very large literal unions or deeply nested alias compositions can slow tsc and the editor, so keep composed types reasonable and split overly complex ones.
productionDeepDive.security: Aliases describe expected shapes but don't validate runtime data. Values from APIs or users should be validated (e.g. with a schema library) before being trusted as a given alias type, since the type is erased.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Encode common patterns once (Nullable<T>, ApiResponse<T>, Status) and reuse the names everywhere; this keeps types consistent and makes domain changes a single, type-checked edit as the codebase grows.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Prefer aliases for unions, tuples, and function types; use interfaces for extensible object/class contracts. Name aliases meaningfully and avoid aliasing trivial types where it adds indirection without value.
productionDeepDive.observability: Alias misuse surfaces in the editor and CI via tsc --noEmit; treating type errors as build failures catches drift between a centralized alias and its usages before runtime.

caseStudies.problem: Inline shapes and unions duplicated across files drifted out of sync, causing bugs and painful refactors.
caseStudies.solution: Centralized named type aliases (status unions, response wrappers) in a shared types module.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: A little indirection (jump-to-definition) versus a single source of truth and one-place edits.
caseStudies.lessons: Name and reuse shared types; use aliases for unions/functions and interfaces for extensible object contracts.

keyTakeaways: A type alias names any type with the type keyword and is erased at compile time (zero runtime cost).
Aliases can name primitives, unions, tuples, object shapes, and function signatures.
Aliasing a primitive doesn't create a distinct type — it's structurally identical and conveys intent only.
Generic type aliases (Nullable<T>, ApiResponse<T>) reuse one definition across many element types.
Use a type alias for unions/tuples/functions and an interface for extensible object/class contracts (see the dedicated interface vs type topic).
